From references to networks

Source: vignettes/articles/from-references-to-networks.qmd

This guide covers the first step of the networkflow pipeline: building the network. It explains what a projected network is, how the similarity between two documents is measured, and which choices (measure, threshold, time windows) shape the network before any cluster is detected. The next guides cover finding and reading clusters and following clusters over time.

Why networks?

Since the 1970s, the number of articles published in most disciplines has grown so much that no historian or sociologist of science can read a whole literature. Citation data offer another entry point: by citing, authors say which works they build on, and the references that articles share reveal groups of works addressing similar questions with similar tools. Mapping these groups, their size and their evolution, has become a common tool of the history and sociology of science, including the history of economics (Claveau and Gingras 2016; Edwards et al. 2018; Cherrier and Svorenčík 2018; Goutsmedt, Claveau, et al. 2023).

networkflow was written for this kind of research. It organises the analysis as a pipeline: building networks from tabular data, detecting clusters, following them over time, naming and plotting them. Each step is a function whose choices are explicit arguments, so that they can be discussed, varied and reported. The functions were developed for, and used in, studies of European macroeconomics (Goutsmedt and Truc 2023), of the explanations of the 1970s stagflation (Goutsmedt 2021), of the history of the concept of rationality (Delcey et al. 2026) and of the scientific reception of a report on the environmental impact of livestock (Duluins et al. 2026).

The example data

The examples use the corpus of Goutsmedt (2021): the books and articles that tried to explain the US stagflation of the 1970s, published between 1975 and 2013, and the references they cite.

library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
nrow(nodes)

Nodes_stagflation has one row per document, Ref_stagflation one row per citation: document source_id cites document target_id. This is the typical shape of research data: not a network, but a table of links between two kinds of entities.

From a two-mode relation to a network

Projection

Citations link two sets of entities: citing documents and cited references. Such a two-mode, or bipartite, relation can be written as a matrix AA with one row per citing document, one column per reference, and aij=1a_{ij} = 1 when document ii cites reference jj. To study the citing documents, we project this relation onto them: two documents are linked when they cite the same references. The raw strength of the tie is the number of shared references,

cik=∑jaijakj=|Ri∩Rk|, c_{ik} = \sum_j a_{ij} a_{kj} = |R_i \cap R_k|,

with RiR_i the bibliography of document ii. In matrix form, C=AA⊤C = A A^\top. This is bibliographic coupling (Kessler 1963): two articles are coupled when their bibliographies overlap. Projecting on the other set gives co-citation (Small 1973): two references are linked when they are cited together, A⊤AA^\top A. The two networks answer different questions. Coupling groups the citing documents, and is fixed once they are published: it maps the research fronts of a period. Co-citation groups the cited works, and evolves as new articles cite them: it maps the intellectual base of a literature as its users see it.

A third relation is often used: direct citation, where documents are linked when one cites the other. It is not a projection (the nodes and the links concern the same entities), so it needs no function of the package: a tbl_graph built from the table of citations among the documents of the corpus can be given directly to add_clusters() and the following steps. Which of the three relations represents a field best has been discussed for a long time, and the answer depends on the criterion. Comparing the clusters obtained on two million biomedical articles, Boyack and Klavans (2010) found that bibliographic coupling slightly outperformed co-citation in representing research fronts, direct citation being the least accurate, with two measures of accuracy (textual coherence and the concentration of grants). With another criterion, the concentration of the references of articles with long bibliographies, Klavans and Boyack (2017) found on the contrary that direct citation was more accurate than coupling and co-citation. Waltman and Eck (2012) built a classification of almost ten million publications on direct citation only, noting that the exclusive reliance on direct citation relations is the main limit of their method, and Rivest et al. (2021) found direct citation, a simple label propagation approach, on par with a deep learning classification of more than 40 million articles. Sjögårde and Ahlgren (2024) show that direct citation networks cluster better when citations are normalised. The relations can also be complementary: for the identification of research topics in computer science, Kleminski et al. (2022) find that bibliographic coupling captures more unique information than direct citation or co-citation, and Yan and Ding (2012) show how the various scholarly networks (coupling, co-citation, co-authorship, co-words) relate to each other. The choice of the relation is therefore a research choice, not a technical one: coupling is well suited to follow what a set of documents cites over time (as here), direct citation to classify very large corpora, co-citation to study the base that a literature draws on. It is worth checking that the main results of a study hold with a second relation.

The same logic applies far beyond citations: authors and the papers they sign (co-authorship), accounts and the hashtags they use, members and the boards they sit on. build_network() projects any such table, given a source_id (the entities that become nodes) and a target_id (the entities that link them).

network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)
network

The result is a tbl_graph from tidygraph: a node table (the columns of nodes) and an edge table (from, to, weight), which can be manipulated with dplyr verbs and drawn with ggraph. Documents without any shared reference are dropped (keep_singleton = FALSE).

Measuring similarity

Raw counts are a poor measure of similarity. An article with 150 references shares some with almost every other article; two short notes sharing three references may be much closer. Normalised measures correct for this. With LiL_i the length of the bibliography of ii, NN the number of citing documents and fjf_j the number of documents citing reference jj, the three measures available through biblionetwork (Goutsmedt, Truc, et al. 2023) are:

  • the coupling angle, the cosine of the two bibliographies (Sen and Gan 1983): wik=|Ri∩Rk|LiLk;w_{ik} = \frac{|R_i \cap R_k|}{\sqrt{L_i L_k}};
  • the coupling strength (Vladutz and Cook 1984; Shen et al. 2019), which gives less weight to the references that everybody cites, in the spirit of the inverse document frequency of text mining: wik=∑j∈Ri∩Rklog⁡(N/fj)LiLk;w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{L_i L_k};
  • the coupling similarity, the idf-weighted cosine of Shen et al. (2019), which normalises the same weighted sum by the weighted length of each bibliography, Si=∑j∈Rilog⁡(N/fj)S_i = \sum_{j \in R_i} \log(N / f_j), as a cosine: wik=∑j∈Ri∩Rklog⁡(N/fj)SiSk.w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{\sqrt{S_i S_k}}.

Sharing a citation of Taylor’s 1993 article on policy rules, cited by 22 documents of the corpus, says less about two explanations of the stagflation than sharing a reference cited by only two: the second and third measures encode this idea.

All measures assume that a work has a single identifier. Raw citation strings do not guarantee it: in Ref_stagflation, Friedman’s 1968 “The Role of Monetary Policy” is written with six different author strings and two titles. Here this is harmless, because the data come with a target_id that the database assigned to each cited work: the 20 citations share the same identifier, and the documents citing it are coupled. Without such an identifier, each spelling would be a different reference, and two documents citing the same work in different ways would not share it. Even with identifiers, matching is never perfect: about 1.5% of the works of Ref_stagflation (28 of 1,856 distinct titles, after removing punctuation and comparing with the year) are attached to more than one target_id. Check the most cited references for duplicates before building a network, and clean them when they matter: the last guide explains why this matters most for co-citation.

How different are the measures in practice? We compute the three networks and compare the weights of the same pairs.

measures <- c("coupling_angle", "coupling_strength", "coupling_similarity")
weights <- lapply(measures, function(measure) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    projection_method = "structured",
    cooccurrence_method = measure,
    edges_threshold = 1
  )
  ids <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes")$source_id
  edges <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "edges")
  data.frame(
    pair = paste(pmin(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to]), pmax(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to])),
    weight = edges$weight
  )
})
pairs <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "pair"), weights)
names(pairs) <- c("pair", measures)
round(cor(pairs[, measures], method = "spearman"), 3)
                    coupling_angle coupling_strength coupling_similarity
coupling_angle               1.000             0.819               0.958
coupling_strength            0.819             1.000               0.884
coupling_similarity          0.958             0.884               1.000

The three measures keep the same pairs (the threshold applies to the raw count) but weight them differently. The coupling similarity is a cosine like the coupling angle, and discounts the common references like the coupling strength: its ranking of the pairs is close to the angle’s (a rank correlation above 0.95) and nearer to the strength’s than the angle’s is. The coupling angle, which treats all references alike, departs most from the coupling strength (a rank correlation of about 0.82). Such a correlation still leaves room for different clusters at the margin: when the conclusions of a study rest on the exact composition of a cluster, it is worth checking them with a second measure. biblionetwork has tools to compare measures on a corpus (compute_couplings(), correlate_weights()).

Thresholds

Most pairs of articles in a literature share one or two classic references. These ties say little, and they make the network dense (edges_threshold = 1 links a quarter of all pairs here). Raising the threshold keeps the pairs that share at least nn references:

thresholds <- data.frame(threshold = 1:4)
thresholds[c("nodes", "edges", "components")] <- t(sapply(thresholds$threshold, function(n) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    projection_method = "structured",
    cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
    edges_threshold = n
  )
  c(igraph::vcount(graph), igraph::ecount(graph), igraph::components(graph)$no)
}))
thresholds
  threshold nodes edges components
1         1   147  2716          1
2         2   131  1501          2
3         3   113   962          4
4         4    99   632          4

Each step removes many edges, but also documents, which no longer share enough references with any other, and breaks the network into components. There is no right threshold: it depends on the length of bibliographies and on the size of the corpus. A threshold of 2 is a common choice for article corpora; in a corpus of short documents with few references, 1 may be the only option.

A statistical alternative: backbones

A threshold is the same for every pair. Yet sharing two references means little for two articles with 150 references each, and a lot for two notes with five. The backbone approach replaces the fixed threshold with a test (Neal 2014): for each pair, is the number of shared targets larger than in random bipartite networks that keep some properties of the observed one? The stochastic degree sequence model (model = "sdsm") keeps, on average, the number of references of each document and the number of citations of each reference; the backbone package (Domagalski et al. 2021; Neal 2022) computes the probabilities.

backbone <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "statistical",
  model = "sdsm",
  alpha = 0.05
)
c(nodes = igraph::vcount(backbone), edges = igraph::ecount(backbone))
nodes edges
  113   553

The backbone keeps the ties that are unlikely under the null model at the 5% level. Its edges are unweighted: each edge means “more shared references than expected”, whatever the number. The approach is slower on large corpora, and with many pairs tested, multiple-test corrections (backbone_args = list(mtc = "holm")) remove many more edges. It is a useful check of a threshold-based network, and the better option when the lengths of the target lists vary a lot.

Components

Projected networks often have one large component and small islands. Community detection and layouts are hard to read on islands, and filter_components() keeps the largest component(s), with a warning if a large one is dropped:

network_2 <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2
)
main_component <- filter_components(network_2)
c(before = igraph::vcount(network_2), after = igraph::vcount(main_component))
before  after
   131    129

Before dropping documents, look at them: a small component may be a marginal literature that matters to the story.

Time windows

A network of the whole period mixes literatures that did not coexist. build_dynamic_networks() builds one network per time window: a window starting in year ss gathers the documents published in [s,s+w−1][s, s + w - 1], ww being time_window, and the network is computed as if the corpus were limited to them. A new window starts every window_step units. By default, windows follow each other (window_step = time_window: 1975-1984, 1985-1994…); with window_step = 1, the window slides by one unit (1975-1984, 1976-1985…); with a step of 5 and a window of 10, each window shares half of its period with the next one. The step is a way to trade resolution in time for computing time and for the number of networks to read.

Months, weeks and days. The unit is the one of the time variable when it is a number. When it is a date (Date, POSIXct, or an ISO date written as text such as "2001-03-15"), time_unit chooses the unit in which windows are counted: "year" (the default), "quarter", "month", "week" or "day". For documents that follow each other quickly, such as the statements of central banks, the question is how many documents a window needs to contain: a network of twenty documents has no structure to detect. With monthly data, a window of 12 months sliding by 3 gives a yearly window every quarter:

build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = statements,            # one row per statement, with a `date` column
  directed_edges = citations,
  source_id = "statement_id",
  target_id = "reference_id",
  time_variable = "date",
  time_unit = "month",
  time_window = 12,
  window_step = 3,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_angle"
)

Windows are named after their first and last unit ("2001-01 to 2001-12" for months, "2001-Q1 to 2001-Q4" for quarters, "1975-1984" for years). The column of the user is never modified.

networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  window_step = 1,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
length(networks)
[1] 30
window_sizes <- data.frame(
  window = names(networks),
  start = as.integer(substr(names(networks), 1, 4)),
  nodes = sapply(networks, igraph::vcount)
)
ggplot(window_sizes, aes(start, nodes)) +
  geom_col(fill = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = window_sizes$start[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    labels = window_sizes$window[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Window", y = "Documents in the main component") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

The size of the windows tells a story of its own: the stagflation was widely debated in the late 1970s and early 1980s, interest faded after the mid-1980s, and a new literature on it emerged in the 1990s, the pattern that Goutsmedt (2021) describes. It also warns about a technical limit: windows centred on the late 1980s contain about ten documents, too few for their clusters to mean much. The choice of the window is substantive. It should be long enough for each network to have enough documents to show a structure, and short enough for changes to be visible. Sliding windows smooth the evolution (consecutive networks share 90% of their period here) and make clusters easier to follow; successive windows give independent snapshots.

What comes next

The networks are ready for community detection. Each choice made here (measure, threshold, window) changes them: report these choices, and check that the main results hold under reasonable alternatives.
